extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners / media relations specialists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for establishing and maintaining effective relations between public relations practitioners and journalists, including what helps/hurts press relations, models of PR behavior, and practical tactics for working with the media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Agentry Abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Most abuses that taint PR's relationship with the press stem from the press agent/publicity model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of press-agentry abuses to avoid: promises to 'deliver' the media; threats to withhold advertising if editors do not use an item or promising to buy advertising if they do; calling a newspaper/broadcast executive to pressure a reporter/editor; sending reams of news releases with little news value to extensive mailing lists of media that have no use for them; mass-mailing releases under the belief that more releases increase random usage; catering to television at the expense of print media (especially at press conferences); mailing releases to out-of-town media when information has no local relevance; sending multiple copies of the same release to different departments or individuals in the same outlet; offering meals/drinks when meetings do not help reporters get needed information; holding press conferences/parties that waste journalists' time when a press release or phone call would suffice; name-dropping or trying to set up conferences for routine releases; excessive checking (phone calls) to confirm receipt of a release; failing to understand how the news media work—deadlines, news values, and beats. (These are anti-patterns; avoid them when evaluating or producing media relations outputs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Information Abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors common to practitioners who act as 'journalists in residence' and follow the public information model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two chief mistakes: (1) The jargon error—writing in the coded language of the organization (often because material must be cleared by superiors) that makes releases unintelligible to journalists; (2) The Parkinson's Law error (Grunig-Hunt corollary)—production of press releases expands to fill available time, leading to unnecessary releases with limited news value. Evaluate materials for plain language and genuine news value; guard against overproduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand how the news media work: deadlines, news values, beats
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective media relations require knowledge of media behavior—deadlines, news values, and beats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must be aware of timing constraints, what editors consider newsworthy, and which reporters cover which beats. Failure to understand these leads to wasted effort (e.g., sending untimely or irrelevant releases). Use this understanding to tailor timing, content, and recipient lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑Way Asymmetric Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Asymmetric practitioners set objectives for what information they want the media to disseminate, but they understand news values and package information journalists will accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended actions for asymmetric practice: stage events or write releases with legitimate news value and articulate the organization's position; rebut erroneous or misleading media information (sometimes via purchased advertising); understand journalist behavior to tailor messages to their communication habits. Be aware asymmetric practice attempts to control coverage and can generate conflict if access is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑Way Symmetric Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetric practitioners open their organization to the media and help journalists cover it, believing openness will yield more accurate and less biased coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize transparency, assistance, and arbitration between management and the press. The role includes making the journalist's job easy by providing substantive facts, packaged conveniently and delivered in good time. Symmetric practice reduces adversarial relationships and focuses on mutual understanding rather than control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the newsman's job easy
rubrics_metrics.description: Key to good press relations strategy is to 'make the newsman's job easy' by giving news of substance with facts he can rely on—conveniently packaged and delivered in good time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This single principle underpins many practical tactics (see related metrics). When evaluating press materials, ask whether they give reliable facts, are well packaged for journalist use, and are timely. Being a reliable source increases likelihood of coverage and trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct contact and fewer, higher‑value releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Send out fewer press releases and rely more on direct contact with journalists (at both their initiative and yours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of mass mailings, call reporters when you have a story that interests them (ensure local angle or relevance). Targeted personal contact is preferable to volume-based distribution. Excessive, low-value releases are counterproductive and waste reporters' time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide interview access and facilitate reporting (don't do the reporting for them)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up interviews for journalists with management or specialists; help reporters cover your organization, but don't attempt to cover it for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange access to knowledgeable sources and provide background so journalists can craft their own stories. Avoid taking over editorial functions; instead enable reporters to do their job accurately and efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concise news 'teasers' or one‑paragraph tips
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer the media one-paragraph news tips (teasers) they can follow up on, rather than only sending full press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Hill & Knowlton's 'News and Feature Leads' newsletter: short leads that inform editors cost-effectively and allow them to request press kits or initiate coverage. Teasers can attract attention more effectively than lengthy, unfocused releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide recorded interviews and accessible background materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview people in your organization, record the interview on cassette (or other media), and provide these recordings and background materials to journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tapes/transcripts, fact sheets, press kits, photos, diagrams, and background information so journalists can integrate primary material into their stories. This reduces misinterpretation and increases accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an information storage and retrieval system for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up an information storage and retrieval system (computerized if possible) containing fact sheets, complete articles, interviews, and background information, and tell journalists what is available and that they may access it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep material updated and inform journalists of its contents and availability. An accessible repository helps reporters verify facts and reduces the time needed for their stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take openness risks but rebut responsibly; never threaten or beg
rubrics_metrics.description: If practicing symmetric relations, take a chance on media accuracy by being open; if miscoverage occurs, provide a rebuttal—but never threaten (e.g., with advertising withdrawal) or beg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openness increases likelihood of fair coverage, but practitioners should be prepared to rebut inaccuracies. Handle rebuttals professionally; avoid coercive tactics which damage credibility and relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segment journalists by information‑seeking behavior and tailor strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists vary: some actively seek information (enterprise reporters), others passively process information (rewrite releases, cover routine events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Grunig's levels of analysis: at the individual level, target reporters with personal interest or bias favorable to your position; at the organizational level, work with editors to assign stories; at the institutional level, stage events and leverage agenda/copying tendencies. Recognize specialized reporters (science, environment, business) are likely to be active and need substantive, detailed information; passive reporters require agenda-setting to put items on their radar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use agenda‑setting as a measurable media relations objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda-setting is essential for setting objectives and evaluating media relations: influencing which issues the media place on their agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the limits of direct attitude change by media, set realistic objectives such as placing topics on the media agenda and measuring coverage/ prominence, rather than expecting strong direct effects on attitudes or behaviors. Use knowledge of mass-media effects to define achievable outcomes.
